title: Planning an Exterior Painting Project
alt: Illustrative painted Ontario home with white siding and charcoal trim
excerpt: A practical starting point for defining the surfaces, finish and scope of your home's next exterior refresh.

sections.title: Start with the whole property
paragraphs: An exterior painting project begins with a clear picture of what you want to change. Walk around your property and note the areas that look faded, uneven or out of step with the rest of your home. Consider the siding, trim, entrance and garage as parts of one overall design.

Keep a simple list of priorities. You may want to refresh the entire exterior, focus on a few visible surfaces, or coordinate new colours with existing stone and roofing. A defined goal makes the first conversation more useful.

sections.title: Separate colour choices from surface condition
paragraphs: A colour scheme is only one part of the plan. Different surfaces and existing finishes need to be assessed before preparation and coatings are selected. Loose paint, damaged materials and areas exposed to moisture should be discussed during the site assessment.

Share what you know about previous painting or repairs. If the history is unclear, say so. A professional assessment should identify what can be included in painting and what may need another repair first.

sections.title: Make the scope easy to compare
paragraphs: Ask for a written description of the areas included, preparation, protection of surrounding surfaces and the proposed coating system. Check whether trim, soffits, fascia, doors and other details are part of the quotation.
Confirm access requirements and how changes to the scope will be handled. Clear written details help you compare proposals on the work being offered rather than on a price alone.

sections.title: Plan access and a final review
paragraphs: Discuss parking, pets, garden furniture and access around your home before work starts. Exterior schedules also depend on suitable conditions, so ask how the team will communicate changes.
Arrange a final walkthrough to review the finished surfaces and care instructions. Keep the agreed colour and product information with your property records for future maintenance.

title: Cabinet Painting or Replacement: Where to Start
alt: Illustrative white shaker kitchen cabinets with a navy island
excerpt: Consider condition, layout and the finish you want before deciding how to refresh your cabinetry.

sections.title: Decide what needs to change
paragraphs: If the kitchen layout works well but the finish feels dated, a cabinet refresh may be worth discussing. Painting changes the appearance of existing cabinetry; replacement can also change the structure, storage and configuration.
Write down the issues you want to solve. Separate colour and finish concerns from damaged boxes, inconvenient storage or a layout that no longer works for your household.

sections.title: Have the existing cabinetry assessed
paragraphs: Doors, drawer fronts, frames and visible panels should be reviewed together. Material, structural condition and previous finishes all influence the proposed work. Not every cabinet is a suitable candidate for the same process.
Ask how repairs, hardware and areas around hinges will be addressed. If additional carpentry is needed, clarify whether it is included or requires a separate contractor.

sections.title: Consider the complete visual finish
paragraphs: Think about how the cabinet colour will relate to the countertops, backsplash, flooring and lighting. Look at samples in your own room rather than relying only on a screen.
Discuss whether the project includes all exposed frames and end panels, as well as doors and drawer fronts. These details can make a significant difference to the overall consistency of the result.

sections.title: Compare the full project scope
paragraphs: Request clear details about preparation, products, access, expected scheduling and the handling of removed components. Ask what will happen if an unexpected condition is found.
The right choice depends on your cabinetry and goals. An assessment and a written scope provide a better starting point than a general promise about price or completion time.

title: Why Surface Preparation Matters
alt: Illustrative gloved worker preparing a cabinet door on a protected bench
excerpt: Understand the preparation questions to ask before an exterior or cabinet painting project begins.

sections.title: Look beyond the final colour
paragraphs: The visible finish is the result of a process. Before choosing a colour, discuss the condition of the surface and the work needed to make it ready for painting. Preparation varies with the material, existing coating and environment.
A professional proposal should explain the approach in terms you can understand. Ask what is being cleaned, repaired or otherwise prepared, and why those steps are appropriate for your project.

sections.title: Discuss repairs and existing finishes
paragraphs: Cracks, loose coatings and damaged components should be identified during assessment. Some conditions can be addressed within the painting scope, while others require repair before painting proceeds.

Tell the team about known leaks, previous repairs and older finishes. Unknown coatings or conditions should be assessed before disturbing them rather than handled through a generic DIY preparation routine.

sections.title: Include protection and access
paragraphs: Preparation also includes planning how nearby surfaces and belongings will be protected. Ask about windows, hardware, countertops, flooring and landscaping as applicable.
Confirm which items you need to move and which areas must remain accessible. A simple preparation conversation can reduce confusion when the team arrives.

sections.title: Ask what is included in writing
paragraphs: A written scope helps establish expectations about preparation, products and the finished surfaces. If the assessment uncovers additional work, ask how it will be documented and agreed.
At the end of the project, review the work together and ask for the relevant care instructions. Preparation and maintenance are both part of planning for a finish you can enjoy over time.

title: Choosing a Colour That Works with Your Home
alt: Illustrative navy front door with brass hardware and white trim
excerpt: Build a coherent palette around the fixed materials, lighting and details already in your space.

sections.title: Begin with the materials that stay
paragraphs: Roofing, brick, stone, counters and flooring are useful starting points for a colour palette. Consider their undertones and how much visual weight they carry in the space.
Collect a few examples of the look you prefer. A small, focused selection is often easier to discuss than a large folder of unrelated styles.

sections.title: Use a simple colour hierarchy
paragraphs: Decide which surface will be the main colour, which details should blend in, and where an accent would be helpful. On an exterior, that might mean siding, trim and a front door. In a kitchen, it might mean the main cabinetry and an island.
A consistent hierarchy helps the finished space feel intentional. You do not need a different colour for every element to create interest.

sections.title: Review samples in the actual space
paragraphs: Screens and photographs can change how a colour appears. Review suitable samples alongside your existing materials and look at them under the lighting you normally experience.
For an exterior, consider the front and less sunny sides of the property. Indoors, look at the palette in daylight and with your usual lamps or ceiling lights.

sections.title: Confirm the colour and finish together
paragraphs: Discuss both colour and finish before approving the project. Surface suitability, product options and sheen should be part of that conversation.
Keep a record of the final colour names, product details and included surfaces. This information helps when you plan future care or discuss additional painting.

title: Caring for a Fresh Paint Finish
alt: Illustrative smooth sage-blue cabinet finish and brass handle
excerpt: Know which care instructions to request and what to record after your painting project is finished.

sections.title: Get instructions for the actual coating
paragraphs: Care guidance should relate to the products and surfaces used in your project. Ask when the area can return to normal use, how to clean it and which products or cleaning methods to avoid.
Do not assume that a surface ready to touch is ready for every kind of use. Follow the specific instructions provided by the painting team and the coating manufacturer.

sections.title: Keep useful project information
paragraphs: Save the colour, sheen and product details, along with the project scope. If touch-ups or further painting are needed later, these records make the conversation easier.
Ask whether leftover material is being supplied and how it should be stored. Follow the product instructions rather than using a general storage rule.

sections.title: Notice changes before they grow
paragraphs: Check painted areas periodically for damage, wear or signs of moisture. Around the exterior, look at places exposed to weather and areas where water could collect. Around cabinetry, pay attention to frequently handled edges and surfaces near sinks.
If you notice a change, discuss the underlying condition before simply repainting it. A finish cannot take the place of a necessary repair.

sections.title: Ask before attempting a repair
paragraphs: An isolated mark and a damaged coating may need different responses. Ask for guidance if you are unsure how to clean or repair the area.
Keep any written warranty or service terms with your records. The applicable scope and terms should come from your own project agreement rather than a general website statement.
